diseases.name: Melanoma
diseases.description: Melanoma is the most serious type of skin cancer. It develops in melanocytes, the cells that produce melanin (the pigment that gives skin its color). Melanoma can develop anywhere on the body, in otherwise normal skin or in an existing mole that becomes cancerous.
symptoms: A new, unusual growth or change in an existing mole
Multiple colors or uneven color distribution
Diameter larger than 6mm (size of a pencil eraser)

abcde.a: Asymmetry: One half of the mole doesn't match the other half
abcde.b: Border: Edges are irregular, ragged, notched, or blurred
abcde.c: Color: The color is not uniform and may include shades of brown, black, pink, red, white, or blue
abcde.d: Diameter: The spot is larger than 6 millimeters across (about ¼ inch – the size of a pencil eraser)
abcde.e: Evolving: The mole is changing in size, shape, or color

riskFactors: Excessive UV exposure from sun or tanning beds
Fair skin, light hair, and light eyes
History of sunburns, especially in childhood
diseases.treatment: Treatment depends on the stage and may include surgical excision, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation therapy, or chemotherapy. Early detection significantly improves outcomes.
prevention: Wear protective clothing and wide-brimmed hats
Seek shade during peak sun hours (10am-4pm)
Get annual skin checks by a dermatologist
diseases.prevalence: Melanoma accounts for about 1% of skin cancers but causes the majority of skin cancer deaths.
diseases.survivalRate: 5-year survival rate is 99% when detected early (localized stage), but drops to 27% for distant metastasis.

diseases.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
diseases.description: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of skin cancer. It arises from the basal cells in the deepest layer of the epidermis. While it rarely metastasizes, it can be locally destructive if left untreated.
symptoms: Pearly or waxy bump on face, ears, or neck
Flat, flesh-colored or brown scar-like lesion
Bleeding or scabbing sore that heals and returns
Pink growth with raised edges and central indentation
White, waxy, scar-like area without clearly defined border

characteristics: Often appears on sun-exposed areas (face, neck, arms)
May have visible blood vessels on surface

diseases.treatment: Treatment options include surgical excision, Mohs surgery, electrodesiccation and curettage, cryotherapy, topical medications, or radiation therapy. Mohs surgery has the highest cure rate (99%).
diseases.prevalence: Most common skin cancer, with over 4 million cases diagnosed annually in the US.
diseases.survivalRate: Cure rate exceeds 95% with proper treatment. Rarely metastasizes but can cause significant local damage.

diseases.name: Actinic Keratoses
diseases.description: Actinic keratoses (AK) are rough, scaly patches on the skin caused by years of sun exposure. They are considered precancerous because they can develop into squamous cell carcinoma if left untreated.
symptoms: Rough, dry, scaly patch of skin
Flat to slightly raised patch or bump
Color variations: pink, red, or brown
Size typically less than 1 inch in diameter

characteristics: Easier to feel than see (rough texture)
Appears on sun-exposed areas (face, scalp, hands, arms)
May come and go, but usually persist

riskFactors: Fair skin, blonde or red hair, blue or green eyes
History of frequent or intense sun exposure
diseases.treatment: Treatment options include cryotherapy (freezing), topical medications (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, diclofenac), chemical peels, photodynamic therapy, or laser therapy.
diseases.prevalence: Affects over 58 million Americans. 10-15% of AKs may progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
diseases.survivalRate: Not applicable (pre-cancerous), but early treatment prevents progression to cancer.

diseases.name: Benign Keratosis
diseases.description: Benign keratosis, commonly seborrheic keratosis, is a non-cancerous skin growth that appears as a waxy, scaly, slightly elevated growth. They are harmless but can be cosmetically concerning.
symptoms: Color ranges from light tan to black
Size varies from very small to over 1 inch

characteristics: Appears to be stuck onto the skin
Common on trunk, face, and shoulders

diseases.treatment: Usually no treatment needed. Can be removed for cosmetic reasons or if irritated using cryotherapy, curettage, or electrocautery.
diseases.prevalence: Very common, affecting over 80 million Americans. Nearly everyone develops at least one by age 60.

diseases.name: Dermatofibroma
diseases.description: Dermatofibroma is a common benign skin growth that appears as a firm, raised bump. It's composed of fibrous tissue and is completely harmless, though it may be cosmetically bothersome.
symptoms: Usually solitary, but can be multiple
riskFactors: Minor skin trauma or insect bites (may trigger formation)
diseases.treatment: Usually no treatment necessary. Can be removed surgically if bothersome, but may leave a scar larger than the original lesion.
diseases.prevalence: Common, affecting millions of people. More frequent in adults.

diseases.name: Melanocytic Nevi
diseases.description: Melanocytic nevi, commonly called moles, are benign growths of melanocytes (pigment-producing cells). Most people have 10-40 moles, and they are usually harmless. However, monitoring for changes is important.
symptoms: Uniform color (brown, tan, black, red, pink, or flesh-colored)

characteristics: Present since childhood or early adulthood

diseases.treatment: No treatment needed unless cosmetically bothersome or showing signs of change. Suspicious moles should be biopsied.
prevention: Sun protection to prevent new moles
Annual skin checks if many moles present
diseases.prevalence: Extremely common. Average adult has 10-40 moles.
diseases.survivalRate: 100% (benign). Risk of melanoma development is very low (<1% lifetime risk per mole).

diseases.name: Vascular Lesions
diseases.description: Vascular lesions are abnormalities of blood vessels in the skin. They include cherry angiomas, spider angiomas, and other benign vascular growths. They are generally harmless.
symptoms: Red or purple spots or bumps
Size varies from pinpoint to several millimeters
diseases.treatment: Usually no treatment needed. Can be removed for cosmetic reasons using laser therapy, electrocautery, or cryotherapy.
prevention: No specific prevention (age and genetics related)
diseases.prevalence: Very common. Cherry angiomas affect over 75% of people over age 75.
